"content": "---\nname: arc-demo-budget-strategy\ndescription: Use when choosing whether to request ARC demos.\nmetadata:\n  hermes:\n    tags: [arc, demonstrations, information-gain]\n    related_skills: [arc-grid-reasoning, arc-demo-hypothesis-audit]\n---\n\n# ARC demo-budget strategy\n\nUse when an ARC task charges for additional demonstrations or has a limited demo budget, particularly when the transformation's selector is unclear. The goal is not to exhaust the available examples; it is to gain enough discriminating evidence for a good decision while controlling request cost.\n\n## Procedure\n\n1. **Parse each pair into evidence.** Record exact changed cells and components, old/new colors, geometry, location, and unchanged alternatives. For object tasks use 4-connected components by default; test 8-connectivity only when diagonal contact could affect the rule.\n2. **Maintain a small explicit hypothesis set.** Phrase candidates as testable selectors and transformations, e.g. “largest non-background component,” “the unique shape matching an exemplar,” or “the component touching the guide line.” Avoid vague accounts like “the interesting object changes.”\n3. **Audit positive and negative examples.** Each hypothesis must predict the selected object in every demo and must not predict edits to observed unchanged objects. Keep object selection and replacement-color mapping as separate questions.\n4. **Plan before requesting.** Name the leading competing hypotheses and what feature of the next pair would distinguish them. If you cannot say how a possible result changes the ranking or action, the request has low information value.\n5. **Track information gain and diminishing returns.** After each demo, note whether hypotheses were eliminated or merely accumulated another compatible case. Do not request again just because a cap remains. If several varied demos fail to isolate a common property, recognize that evidence may be saturated or underdetermined.\n6. **Choose request vs submit by expected cost.** Request only when the next example could plausibly distinguish materially different rules and its expected value justifies its score cost versus a likely-wrong submission. If no useful request remains, make the best-supported deliberate choice rather than spending by default.\n7. **Preserve uncertainty.** Reaching the demo cap does not validate a guess. If the selector remains ambiguous, do not claim a visually plausible candidate is established; alter only cells warranted by the strongest supported hypothesis.\n8. **Honor the task interface.** When the environment requires exactly one JSON action, return exactly one action and no surrounding explanation.\n\n## Evidence ledger for changed-component tasks\n\n| Pair | Changed component | Before → after | Area / geometry | Position | Unchanged candidates |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n\nInclude unchanged same-color components and similar shapes. This guards against largest/smallest-object and color-only fallacies. `arc-demo-hypothesis-audit` has broader component auditing guidance; this skill focuses on deciding when an additional example is worth its cost.\n\n## Continual-ARC lesson: task-fba999ff\n\nThree requested demonstrations sufficed to identify the transform: connect same-color cells sharing a row or column by recoloring only strict interior cells to 3; endpoints and other cells remain unchanged. Demo palettes/backgrounds varied, while connector color stayed 3. In the fresh 5x25 test, only the two 8-markers at row 1, columns 12 and 14 had a gap, so one cell changed. Adjacent aligned marker pairs create no interior. This example rewarded careful sparse test audit; no fourth demo was needed after pair 3 showed extensive row/column segment completion and the test's sole gap was unambiguous.\n\n## Continual-ARC note: task-b335a605 tiny horizontal-band case\n\nOne test's unchanged-grid guess was wrong: the 4×4 input had full rows `[0,0,0,0]`, `[4,4,4,4]`, `[4,4,4,4]`, `[6,6,6,6]`. One demo showed a 7×7 analog where only the leading all-zero row changed, becoming the color of the bottom row (4); all other full-width bands, including duplicate adjacent colors, stayed exactly as input. The accepted test changed its top row to 6 (bottom-row color) and preserved all other rows. This is one branch-specific example, not a universal rule for task-b335a605: the task ID also recurs with periodic diagonal and horizontal patterns. A targeted demo was worth its cost because no-op and leading-row-from-bottom hypotheses predicted different outputs. See `puzzles:arc-grid-reasoning` reference `task-b335a605-tiny-horizontal-bands.md`.\n\n## Continual-ARC note: task-b335a605 horizontal stripe residues\n\nA separate accepted 28×28 instance with three nonzero full-width stripes (row 0 color 5, row 4 color 3, row 20 color 7) used stripe count `k=3` as the vertical period: each stripe's color fills its row residue modulo 3, yielding repeated `[5,3,7]`. Three demos supported this rule with different stripe counts/palettes; crucially, line colors are keyed by row modulo stripe count, not by numeric ordering. This is a separate recurrence branch from the tiny leading-row case and from diagonal periodic variants. See `puzzles:arc-grid-reasoning` reference `task-b335a605-horizontal-row-residue-pattern.md`.\n\n## Accepted recurrence note: task-2e5d2205 paired vertical edge runs (25×6)\n\nA fresh test with no demos was accepted with zero wrong submissions, adding confirmation to the paired equal-length opposing-edge-run branch: background 6; color-3 vertical runs of length 4 at right edge rows 0–3 and left edge rows 19–22; color-7 markers in the left run at `(20,3),(21,4),(22,2)`. Markers became 4 and their rows filled with 7 inward toward the left edge (c1–2, c1–3, c1), preserving edge 3. Corresponding offsets in the opposite right-edge run filled rows 1–3 across c0–4, preserving right edge 3; row 0 and all unselected rows remained unchanged. See `arc-ray-projection/references/task-2e5d2205-edge-run-correspondence-25x6-accepted.md` for the exact accepted grid. This reinforces the paired equal-length-run rule only; do not apply it to geometrically different unresolved recurrences with the same ID.\n\n## Unsolved recurrence note: task-7c19c728 with mixed diagonal pairs\n\nA 25×6 test was not solved after eight wrong submissions and two demos, despite two demos supporting diagonal same-color pair rays. Input (0-based) contained background 3; 4 at `(21,4),(22,3)`, 9 at `(22,2),(23,3)`, and 1 at `(23,2),(24,1)`. Demo 1 extended a 7-pair down-left and a 4-pair down-right; demo 2 extended a 6-pair down-left, painting through background until edge/blocker. Applying the apparent ray rule to the 9 and 4 pairs predicted 9 at `(20,0),(21,1),(24,4)` and 4 at `(20,5)`. This was rejected, including after removing the mistaken extra 4 at `(21,5)`; no candidate was accepted. The 1 pair appeared blocked on one side and boundary-limited on the other, but its exact relevance is unresolved. Treat this as uncertainty/negative evidence, not a validated transformation or selector. For future instances with multiple mixed-color/overlapping pairs, request a targeted demo before committing; do not overinterpret binary rejections.\n\n## Continual-ARC recurrence note: task-b335a605 periodic diagonal-stripe completion\n\nA solved fresh instance (19×19, zero wrong submissions) and four varied demos establish a diagonal-stripe periodic fill branch. Treat this separately from the task ID's horizontal stripe-residue and tiny horizontal-band branches: recurring IDs may present different transformations on fresh inputs.\n\n**Rule supported by these pairs:** Identify the parallel colored diagonals and their integer intercept/index. For down-right diagonals use `c-r`; for down-left diagonals use `r+c`. Find the smallest positive period `p` for which every observed diagonal index congruent modulo `p` has a consistent color. Fill every cell by the color assigned to its diagonal-index residue. Preserve the input dimensions. If a residue is represented by multiple observed lines, their colors must agree; do not impose an unobserved palette ordering.\n\n**Evidence ledger:**\n- Demo 1 (12×12): down-right diagonals; observed `c-r` indices 0→3, 4→4, 7→2, 8→6, 11→8. The output is periodic in `c-r` with period 6; residues 0…5 map `[3,2,6,6,4,8]`.\n- Demo 2 (29×29): only color-2 diagonals were marked; output is uniformly 2, consistent with the minimum period 1.\n- Demo 3 (22×22): down-left diagonals; `r+c` indices 1→5, 2→6, 7→8, 28→9. Output repeats with period 4, mapping residues 0…3 to `[9,5,6,8]`.\n- Demo 4 (28×28): down-right diagonals; `c-r` indices 14→3, −4→6, −21→6, −27→8. Output repeats with period 4, mapping residues 0…3 to `[6,8,3,6]`.\n- Accepted test (19×19): down-left diagonals with sums 3→1, 9→8, 19→9, 25→6, 27→4, 29→4, 35→2. Smallest consistent period is 7; residues 0…6 map `[2,4,8,1,6,9,4]`. Accepted output is `out[r][c] = map[(r+c) mod 7]`.\n\n**Practical caution:** infer orientation from the marked diagonals (slope), not from a favored formula. Use the smallest consistent modular period rather than guessing the grid width or number of colored cells. A single-color example cannot distinguish periods and only supports the constant-color special case; when multicolor input lines permit materially different periods, a targeted demo can be useful. This is direct task-ID recurrence evidence, not a universal ARC rule.\n\n## Common pitfalls\n\n- **Demo-cap completionism:** treating all available requests as a target rather than a limit.\n- **Unspecified information gain:** requesting “another example” without naming what uncertainty it could resolve.\n- **Positive-only reasoning:** tracking only the changed object, not unchanged lookalikes.\n- **Selector/mapping conflation:** guessing the output color while still unsure which object is selected.\n- **Binary-feedback overreach:** interpreting a rejected full-grid submission as identifying a particular wrong cell or assumption.\n- **False certainty after saturation:** mistaking a long list of varied examples for a discovered rule when no common discriminating property has been tested.\n\nFor the recurring component-recoloring case where eight demonstrations did not establish a selector, see `references/unresolved-component-recoloring.md`.", "path": "content": "---\nname: arc-demo-budget-strategy\ndescription: Use when choosing whether to request ARC demos.\nmetadata:\n  hermes:\n    tags: [arc, demonstrations, information-gain]\n    related_skills: [arc-grid-reasoning, arc-demo-hypothesis-audit]\n---\n\n# ARC demo-budget strategy\n\nUse when an ARC task charges for additional demonstrations or has a limited demo budget, particularly when the transformation's selector is unclear. The goal is not to exhaust the available examples; it is to gain enough discriminating evidence for a good decision while controlling request cost.\n\n## Procedure\n\n1. **Parse each pair into evidence.** Record exact changed cells and components, old/new colors, geometry, location, and unchanged alternatives. For object tasks use 4-connected components by default; test 8-connectivity only when diagonal contact could affect the rule.\n2. **Maintain a small explicit hypothesis set.** Phrase candidates as testable selectors and transformations, e.g. “largest non-background component,” “the unique shape matching an exemplar,” or “the component touching the guide line.” Avoid vague accounts like “the interesting object changes.”\n3. **Audit positive and negative examples.** Each hypothesis must predict the selected object in every demo and must not predict edits to observed unchanged objects. Keep object selection and replacement-color mapping as separate questions.\n4. **Plan before requesting.** Name the leading competing hypotheses and what feature of the next pair would distinguish them. If you cannot say how a possible result changes the ranking or action, the request has low information value.\n5. **Track information gain and diminishing returns.** After each demo, note whether hypotheses were eliminated or merely accumulated another compatible case. Do not request again just because a cap remains. If several varied demos fail to isolate a common property, recognize that evidence may be saturated or underdetermined.\n6. **Choose request vs submit by expected cost.** Request only when the next example could plausibly distinguish materially different rules and its expected value justifies its score cost versus a likely-wrong submission. If no useful request remains, make the best-supported deliberate choice rather than spending by default.\n7. **Preserve uncertainty.** Reaching the demo cap does not validate a guess. If the selector remains ambiguous, do not claim a visually plausible candidate is established; alter only cells warranted by the strongest supported hypothesis.\n8. **Honor the task interface.** When the environment requires exactly one JSON action, return exactly one action and no surrounding explanation.\n\n## Evidence ledger for changed-component tasks\n\n| Pair | Changed component | Before → after | Area / geometry | Position | Unchanged candidates |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n\nInclude unchanged same-color components and similar shapes. This guards against largest/smallest-object and color-only fallacies. `arc-demo-hypothesis-audit` has broader component auditing guidance; this skill focuses on deciding when an additional example is worth its cost.\n\n## Continual-ARC lesson: task-fba999ff\n\nThree requested demonstrations sufficed to identify the transform: connect same-color cells sharing a row or column by recoloring only strict interior cells to 3; endpoints and other cells remain unchanged. Demo palettes/backgrounds varied, while connector color stayed 3. In the fresh 5x25 test, only the two 8-markers at row 1, columns 12 and 14 had a gap, so one cell changed. Adjacent aligned marker pairs create no interior. This example rewarded careful sparse test audit; no fourth demo was needed after pair 3 showed extensive row/column segment completion and the test's sole gap was unambiguous.\n\n## Continual-ARC note: task-b335a605 tiny horizontal-band case\n\nOne test's unchanged-grid guess was wrong: the 4×4 input had full rows `[0,0,0,0]`, `[4,4,4,4]`, `[4,4,4,4]`, `[6,6,6,6]`. One demo showed a 7×7 analog where only the leading all-zero row changed, becoming the color of the bottom row (4); all other full-width bands, including duplicate adjacent colors, stayed exactly as input. The accepted test changed its top row to 6 (bottom-row color) and preserved all other rows. This is one branch-specific example, not a universal rule for task-b335a605: the task ID also recurs with periodic diagonal and horizontal patterns. A targeted demo was worth its cost because no-op and leading-row-from-bottom hypotheses predicted different outputs. See `puzzles:arc-grid-reasoning` reference `task-b335a605-tiny-horizontal-bands.md`.\n\n## Continual-ARC note: task-b335a605 horizontal stripe residues\n\nA separate accepted 28×28 instance with three nonzero full-width stripes (row 0 color 5, row 4 color 3, row 20 color 7) used stripe count `k=3` as the vertical period: each stripe's color fills its row residue modulo 3, yielding repeated `[5,3,7]`. Three demos supported this rule with different stripe counts/palettes; crucially, line colors are keyed by row modulo stripe count, not by numeric ordering. This is a separate recurrence branch from the tiny leading-row case and from diagonal periodic variants. See `puzzles:arc-grid-reasoning` reference `task-b335a605-horizontal-row-residue-pattern.md`.\n\n## Accepted recurrence note: task-2e5d2205 paired vertical edge runs (25×6)\n\nA fresh test with no demos was accepted with zero wrong submissions, adding confirmation to the paired equal-length opposing-edge-run branch: background 6; color-3 vertical runs of length 4 at right edge rows 0–3 and left edge rows 19–22; color-7 markers in the left run at `(20,3),(21,4),(22,2)`. Markers became 4 and their rows filled with 7 inward toward the left edge (c1–2, c1–3, c1), preserving edge 3. Corresponding offsets in the opposite right-edge run filled rows 1–3 across c0–4, preserving right edge 3; row 0 and all unselected rows remained unchanged. See `arc-ray-projection/references/task-2e5d2205-edge-run-correspondence-25x6-accepted.md` for the exact accepted grid. This reinforces the paired equal-length-run rule only; do not apply it to geometrically different unresolved recurrences with the same ID.\n\n## Unsolved recurrence note: task-7c19c728 with mixed diagonal pairs\n\nA 25×6 test was not solved after eight wrong submissions and two demos, despite two demos supporting diagonal same-color pair rays. Input (0-based) contained background 3; 4 at `(21,4),(22,3)`, 9 at `(22,2),(23,3)`, and 1 at `(23,2),(24,1)`. Demo 1 extended a 7-pair down-left and a 4-pair down-right; demo 2 extended a 6-pair down-left, painting through background until edge/blocker. Applying the apparent ray rule to the 9 and 4 pairs predicted 9 at `(20,0),(21,1),(24,4)` and 4 at `(20,5)`. This was rejected, including after removing the mistaken extra 4 at `(21,5)`; no candidate was accepted. The 1 pair appeared blocked on one side and boundary-limited on the other, but its exact relevance is unresolved. Treat this as uncertainty/negative evidence, not a validated transformation or selector. For future instances with multiple mixed-color/overlapping pairs, request a targeted demo before committing; do not overinterpret binary rejections.\n\n## Continual-ARC recurrence note: task-b335a605 periodic diagonal-stripe completion\n\nA solved fresh instance (19×19, zero wrong submissions) and four varied demos establish a diagonal-stripe periodic fill branch. Treat this separately from the task ID's horizontal stripe-residue and tiny horizontal-band branches: recurring IDs may present different transformations on fresh inputs.\n\n**Rule supported by these pairs:** Identify the parallel colored diagonals and their integer intercept/index. For down-right diagonals use `c-r`; for down-left diagonals use `r+c`. Find the smallest positive period `p` for which every observed diagonal index congruent modulo `p` has a consistent color. Fill every cell by the color assigned to its diagonal-index residue. Preserve the input dimensions. If a residue is represented by multiple observed lines, their colors must agree; do not impose an unobserved palette ordering.\n\n**Evidence ledger:**\n- Demo 1 (12×12): down-right diagonals; observed `c-r` indices 0→3, 4→4, 7→2, 8→6, 11→8. The output is periodic in `c-r` with period 6; residues 0…5 map `[3,2,6,6,4,8]`.\n- Demo 2 (29×29): only color-2 diagonals were marked; output is uniformly 2, consistent with the minimum period 1.\n- Demo 3 (22×22): down-left diagonals; `r+c` indices 1→5, 2→6, 7→8, 28→9. Output repeats with period 4, mapping residues 0…3 to `[9,5,6,8]`.\n- Demo 4 (28×28): down-right diagonals; `c-r` indices 14→3, −4→6, −21→6, −27→8. Output repeats with period 4, mapping residues 0…3 to `[6,8,3,6]`.\n- Accepted test (19×19): down-left diagonals with sums 3→1, 9→8, 19→9, 25→6, 27→4, 29→4, 35→2. Smallest consistent period is 7; residues 0…6 map `[2,4,8,1,6,9,4]`. Accepted output is `out[r][c] = map[(r+c) mod 7]`.\n\n**Practical caution:** infer orientation from the marked diagonals (slope), not from a favored formula. Use the smallest consistent modular period rather than guessing the grid width or number of colored cells. A single-color example cannot distinguish periods and only supports the constant-color special case; when multicolor input lines permit materially different periods, a targeted demo can be useful. This is direct task-ID recurrence evidence, not a universal ARC rule.\n\n## Common pitfalls\n\n- **Demo-cap completionism:** treating all available requests as a target rather than a limit.\n- **Unspecified information gain:** requesting “another example” without naming what uncertainty it could resolve.\n- **Positive-only reasoning:** tracking only the changed object, not unchanged lookalikes.\n- **Selector/mapping conflation:** guessing the output color while still unsure which object is selected.\n- **Binary-feedback overreach:** interpreting a rejected full-grid submission as identifying a particular wrong cell or assumption.\n- **False certainty after saturation:** mistaking a long list of varied examples for a discovered rule when no common discriminating property has been tested.\n\nFor the recurring component-recoloring case where eight demonstrations did not establish a selector, see `references/unresolved-component-recoloring.md`.", "path": # ARC demo action discipline

For ARC streams where demos and submissions each consume score or attempts, make an evidence-based choice after every returned example. Never turn demo requests into an automatic chain.

## Per-pair loop

1. **Parse the complete pair.** Compare input/output cell by cell. Record changed coordinates, connected components (4-connectivity by default), old/new colors, shape, and location. Record unchanged lookalike objects as negative evidence.
2. **Separate selector from transformation.** Maintain testable hypotheses for which component(s) are selected separately from color/geometry mapping. Each hypothesis must explain changed and unchanged examples.
3. **Re-evaluate the test now.** Identify test objects selected by each surviving rule and the predicted output. Do not delay this because demo capacity remains.
4. **Gate the next request.** Before asking for a pair, name at least two materially different hypotheses and a plausible feature of the next demo that would distinguish them; say how each outcome changes the test prediction. If no concrete distinction can be stated, stop requesting and submit the best-supported answer.
5. **Account for diminishing returns and costs.** A new varied example that only adds another selected object without clarifying a common selector does not justify another request. Compare the request's cost with likely wrong-submission cost. Uncertainty is not itself information gain.
6. **After rejection, audit the whole candidate.** Binary feedback does not locate the error; reconsider selector, mapping, segmentation, and preservation. Change only a reasoned assumption, not a salient object/color at random.

## Continual-ARC recurrence note: task-51a4dd40 fresh 15×15 patterned bands

A fresh 15×15 instance was accepted after eight varied demos and one rejected candidate. All demos used replacement color 1, but contextual selection remains unresolved; do not apply a generic suffix/continuation rule. See `references/task-51a4dd40-fresh-15x15-two-band-accepted.md` for the complete delta ledger and accepted test coordinates. The accepted test changed exactly rows 9–10, columns 13–14 (zero-based) from background 0 to 1; the first rejected version omitted row 10 column 13. Preserve this as exact instance evidence only, not a general selector for future task-ID recurrences.

## Known transform family: sealed background holes

For a demonstrated pattern where a background-color pocket is enclosed by non-background linework, use 4-neighbor flood-fill from the grid edge: preserve reachable exterior background, recolor enclosed background pockets to the demonstrated replacement color, and preserve all linework. A validated recurrence with exact demo and test evidence is recorded in `puzzles/arc-grid-reasoning/references/task-66859c98-sealed-background-holes.md`. Do not infer this rule without checking the current task's examples; background/frame palette can vary.

## Ledger

| Pair | Changed objects | Before → after | Selector evidence | Unchanged counterexamples | Test prediction |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

For many-object recoloring, treat disconnected same-color components as distinct unless examples establish color-wide treatment.

## Pitfalls

- **Automatic demo chaining:** requesting immediately after a pair without an evidence review.
- **Demo-cap completionism:** exhausting requests just because they are available.
- **Positive-only reasoning:** ignoring unchanged lookalikes.
- **Selector/mapping conflation:** choosing a replacement color while target selection is unresolved.
- **Plausibility as proof:** choosing a visually prominent test object without a selector supported by all examples.
- **Binary-feedback overreach:** interpreting a wrong full-grid submission as diagnosis of one cell or assumption.

# ARC demo-budget strategy

Use when an ARC task charges for additional demonstrations or has a limited demo budget, particularly when the transformation's selector is unclear. The goal is not to exhaust the available examples; it is to gain enough discriminating evidence for a good decision while controlling request cost.

## Procedure

1. **Parse each pair into evidence.** Record exact changed cells and components, old/new colors, geometry, location, and unchanged alternatives. For object tasks use 4-connected components by default; test 8-connectivity only when diagonal contact could affect the rule.
2. **Maintain a small explicit hypothesis set.** Phrase candidates as testable selectors and transformations, e.g. “largest non-background component,” “the unique shape matching an exemplar,” or “the component touching the guide line.” Avoid vague accounts like “the interesting object changes.”
3. **Audit positive and negative examples.** Each hypothesis must predict the selected object in every demo and must not predict edits to observed unchanged objects. Keep object selection and replacement-color mapping as separate questions.
4. **Plan before requesting.** Name the leading competing hypotheses and what feature of the next pair would distinguish them. If you cannot say how a possible result changes the ranking or action, the request has low information value.
5. **Track information gain and diminishing returns.** After each demo, note whether hypotheses were eliminated or merely accumulated another compatible case. Do not request again just because a cap remains. If several varied demos fail to isolate a common property, recognize that evidence may be saturated or underdetermined.
6. **Choose request vs submit by expected cost.** Request only when the next example could plausibly distinguish materially different rules and its expected value justifies its score cost versus a likely-wrong submission. If no useful request remains, make the best-supported deliberate choice rather than spending by default.
7. **Preserve uncertainty.** Reaching the demo cap does not validate a guess. If the selector remains ambiguous, do not claim a visually plausible candidate is established; alter only cells warranted by the strongest supported hypothesis.
8. **Honor the task interface.** When the environment requires exactly one JSON action, return exactly one action and no surrounding explanation.

## Evidence ledger for changed-component tasks

| Pair | Changed component | Before → after | Area / geometry | Position | Unchanged candidates |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

Include unchanged same-color components and similar shapes. This guards against largest/smallest-object and color-only fallacies. `arc-demo-hypothesis-audit` has broader component auditing guidance; this skill focuses on deciding when an additional example is worth its cost.

## Continual-ARC lesson: task-fba999ff

Three requested demonstrations sufficed to identify the transform: connect same-color cells sharing a row or column by recoloring only strict interior cells to 3; endpoints and other cells remain unchanged. Demo palettes/backgrounds varied, while connector color stayed 3. In the fresh 5x25 test, only the two 8-markers at row 1, columns 12 and 14 had a gap, so one cell changed. Adjacent aligned marker pairs create no interior. This example rewarded careful sparse test audit; no fourth demo was needed after pair 3 showed extensive row/column segment completion and the test's sole gap was unambiguous.

## Continual-ARC note: task-b335a605 tiny horizontal-band case

One test's unchanged-grid guess was wrong: the 4×4 input had full rows `[0,0,0,0]`, `[4,4,4,4]`, `[4,4,4,4]`, `[6,6,6,6]`. One demo showed a 7×7 analog where only the leading all-zero row changed, becoming the color of the bottom row (4); all other full-width bands, including duplicate adjacent colors, stayed exactly as input. The accepted test changed its top row to 6 (bottom-row color) and preserved all other rows. This is one branch-specific example, not a universal rule for task-b335a605: the task ID also recurs with periodic diagonal and horizontal patterns. A targeted demo was worth its cost because no-op and leading-row-from-bottom hypotheses predicted different outputs. See `puzzles:arc-grid-reasoning` reference `task-b335a605-tiny-horizontal-bands.md`.

## Continual-ARC note: task-b335a605 horizontal stripe residues

A separate accepted 28×28 instance with three nonzero full-width stripes (row 0 color 5, row 4 color 3, row 20 color 7) used stripe count `k=3` as the vertical period: each stripe's color fills its row residue modulo 3, yielding repeated `[5,3,7]`. Three demos supported this rule with different stripe counts/palettes; crucially, line colors are keyed by row modulo stripe count, not by numeric ordering. This is a separate recurrence branch from the tiny leading-row case and from diagonal periodic variants. See `puzzles:arc-grid-reasoning` reference `task-b335a605-horizontal-row-residue-pattern.md`.

## Accepted recurrence note: task-2e5d2205 paired vertical edge runs (25×6)

A fresh test with no demos was accepted with zero wrong submissions, adding confirmation to the paired equal-length opposing-edge-run branch: background 6; color-3 vertical runs of length 4 at right edge rows 0–3 and left edge rows 19–22; color-7 markers in the left run at `(20,3),(21,4),(22,2)`. Markers became 4 and their rows filled with 7 inward toward the left edge (c1–2, c1–3, c1), preserving edge 3. Corresponding offsets in the opposite right-edge run filled rows 1–3 across c0–4, preserving right edge 3; row 0 and all unselected rows remained unchanged. See `arc-ray-projection/references/task-2e5d2205-edge-run-correspondence-25x6-accepted.md` for the exact accepted grid. This reinforces the paired equal-length-run rule only; do not apply it to geometrically different unresolved recurrences with the same ID.

## Unsolved recurrence note: task-7c19c728 with mixed diagonal pairs

A 25×6 test was not solved after eight wrong submissions and two demos, despite two demos supporting diagonal same-color pair rays. Input (0-based) contained background 3; 4 at `(21,4),(22,3)`, 9 at `(22,2),(23,3)`, and 1 at `(23,2),(24,1)`. Demo 1 extended a 7-pair down-left and a 4-pair down-right; demo 2 extended a 6-pair down-left, painting through background until edge/blocker. Applying the apparent ray rule to the 9 and 4 pairs predicted 9 at `(20,0),(21,1),(24,4)` and 4 at `(20,5)`. This was rejected, including after removing the mistaken extra 4 at `(21,5)`; no candidate was accepted. The 1 pair appeared blocked on one side and boundary-limited on the other, but its exact relevance is unresolved. Treat this as uncertainty/negative evidence, not a validated transformation or selector. For future instances with multiple mixed-color/overlapping pairs, request a targeted demo before committing; do not overinterpret binary rejections.

## Continual-ARC recurrence note: task-b335a605 periodic diagonal-stripe completion

A solved fresh instance (19×19, zero wrong submissions) and four varied demos establish a diagonal-stripe periodic fill branch. Treat this separately from the task ID's horizontal stripe-residue and tiny horizontal-band branches: recurring IDs may present different transformations on fresh inputs.

**Rule supported by these pairs:** Identify the parallel colored diagonals and their integer intercept/index. For down-right diagonals use `c-r`; for down-left diagonals use `r+c`. Find the smallest positive period `p` for which every observed diagonal index congruent modulo `p` has a consistent color. Fill every cell by the color assigned to its diagonal-index residue. Preserve the input dimensions. If a residue is represented by multiple observed lines, their colors must agree; do not impose an unobserved palette ordering.

**Evidence ledger:**
- Demo 1 (12×12): down-right diagonals; observed `c-r` indices 0→3, 4→4, 7→2, 8→6, 11→8. The output is periodic in `c-r` with period 6; residues 0…5 map `[3,2,6,6,4,8]`.
- Demo 2 (29×29): only color-2 diagonals were marked; output is uniformly 2, consistent with the minimum period 1.
- Demo 3 (22×22): down-left diagonals; `r+c` indices 1→5, 2→6, 7→8, 28→9. Output repeats with period 4, mapping residues 0…3 to `[9,5,6,8]`.
- Demo 4 (28×28): down-right diagonals; `c-r` indices 14→3, −4→6, −21→6, −27→8. Output repeats with period 4, mapping residues 0…3 to `[6,8,3,6]`.
- Accepted test (19×19): down-left diagonals with sums 3→1, 9→8, 19→9, 25→6, 27→4, 29→4, 35→2. Smallest consistent period is 7; residues 0…6 map `[2,4,8,1,6,9,4]`. Accepted output is `out[r][c] = map[(r+c) mod 7]`.

**Practical caution:** infer orientation from the marked diagonals (slope), not from a favored formula. Use the smallest consistent modular period rather than guessing the grid width or number of colored cells. A single-color example cannot distinguish periods and only supports the constant-color special case; when multicolor input lines permit materially different periods, a targeted demo can be useful. This is direct task-ID recurrence evidence, not a universal ARC rule.

## Common pitfalls

- **Demo-cap completionism:** treating all available requests as a target rather than a limit.
- **Unspecified information gain:** requesting “another example” without naming what uncertainty it could resolve.
- **Positive-only reasoning:** tracking only the changed object, not unchanged lookalikes.
- **Selector/mapping conflation:** guessing the output color while still unsure which object is selected.

# ARC demonstration hypothesis audit

## When to Use

Use this skill when demonstrations establish that only some components change, or when multiple plausible rules fit the examples. Often the hard part is identifying **which object** changes, not applying a known transformation. Do not let visual prominence, color, or size stand in for a demonstrated rule.

## Evidence-first workflow

1. **Parse every grid and object.** Identify background, 4-connected components, and when useful 8-connected groupings. Record each component's color, cells/bounding box, area, shape, orientation, and location. Disconnected components of one color can have distinct roles.
2. **Compute exact deltas.** For every demo, list all changed coordinates and before/after colors. Group changed coordinates into components and note source/template effects. Record unchanged candidates too; these negative examples are evidence.
3. **Maintain an evidence ledger.** Suggested columns: demo, changed component, old→new color, shape/area, related objects, plausible distinguishing property. Avoid claims like “the small shape changes” unless other small shapes are explicitly ruled out.
4. **Test hypotheses against all candidates.** Phrase competing rules as testable selection conditions (exact shape match, relative size, orientation, adjacency, containment, object role). Predict every changed and unchanged component in each demo. Eliminate rules that do not account for unchanged alternatives.
5. **Request demos for information gain.** Before a request, name competing hypotheses and what example would distinguish them. Requests cost score; do not ask just because uncertain. Do not submit a weak guess if another demo could distinguish candidates.
6. **Apply only the validated rule.** Identify the exact test component through the criterion established by the ledger; derive its mapped color/geometry separately. Preserve other cells unless demos show more changes.
7. **After rejection, audit the mapping first.** Binary feedback can mean wrong object, color, scope, connectivity, or transformation. Re-parse and compare every demo delta. Do not cycle through prominent candidate objects on the same unsupported premise; change one evidence-backed assumption at a time.
8. **Validate mechanically.** Check grid height, row widths, values 0–9, exact changed-cell set, untouched regions, and strict action-interface formatting.

## Common failures

- **Prominence fallacy:** selecting the largest or most conspicuous object without evidence that size/prominence is the selector.
- **Loose relation:** “small object becomes the large object's color” fits a couple of examples but fails to explain all changed and unchanged alternatives.
- **Color-only mapping:** recoloring every occurrence of a color when demos changed only one connected component.
- **Component conflation:** treating disconnected same-color regions as one object, or assuming adjacent cells of different colors form a component.
- **Post-rejection random walk:** trying another object/color without explaining how feedback changes the hypothesis ranking.
- **Overinterpreting binary feedback:** rejection marks the complete candidate output wrong but identifies no particular cell or assumption.
